title: Academic Reading — Practice test 1

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.heading: Bees on the Rooftops

vocab.ex: the idea of keeping bees in the middle of a large city would have struck most people as eccentric
the well-publicised decline of bee populations in the countryside

vocab.vi: bị chi phối / chiếm phần lớn bởi
vocab.ex: farmland is often dominated by a single crop that blooms for only a few weeks
city gardeners use far fewer pesticides than commercial farmers
a distinctive minty flavour, which they attribute to the lime trees
urban honey generally contains lower levels of pesticide residue
it is by no means the most endangered
Wild bees, many of which live alone rather than in colonies, are far more vulnerable to the loss of habitat
Because honeybees forage in large numbers

vocab.vi: đàn (ong, côn trùng) bay thành đám
vocab.ex: a swarm of several thousand bees landing on a busy shopping street can cause alarm
Such measures benefit all pollinators, not just honeybees

paragraphs: Ten years ago, the idea of keeping bees in the middle of a large city would have struck most people as eccentric. Today, hives can be found on the roofs of hotels, office blocks and even fire stations in cities from London to Tokyo. In Paris alone, the number of registered hives rose from around 300 in 2010 to more than 2,000 a decade later. Supporters see urban beekeeping as a small but meaningful response to the well-publicised decline of bee populations in the countryside.

Cities turn out to be surprisingly good places for bees. Because parks, gardens, balconies and roadside verges are planted with a wide variety of species, flowers are available for much of the year, whereas farmland is often dominated by a single crop that blooms for only a few weeks. Urban areas are also, on average, two or three degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, which allows colonies to remain active for longer. Perhaps most importantly, city gardeners use far fewer pesticides than commercial farmers, and these chemicals are widely believed to be one of the main causes of colony losses.

The honey produced in cities has its own character. Beekeepers in Berlin, for example, report that their honey has a distinctive minty flavour, which they attribute to the lime trees that line many of the city's streets. Laboratory tests carried out in several European capitals have found that urban honey generally contains lower levels of pesticide residue than honey from rural areas, although it can contain small amounts of heavy metals from traffic. In most cases these levels are well below the limits set by food safety authorities.

However, not everyone is convinced that the trend is entirely positive. Some ecologists point out that the honeybee is only one of more than 20,000 bee species, and it is by no means the most endangered. Wild bees, many of which live alone rather than in colonies, are far more vulnerable to the loss of habitat. Because honeybees forage in large numbers, a high density of hives can leave less nectar and pollen for these wild species. A study in London found that the amount of food available per hive in the city had fallen sharply as the number of hives grew, and the researchers warned that the city may already be approaching its limit.

Keeping bees responsibly also requires more skill than many newcomers expect. Colonies must be inspected regularly for disease, and a poorly managed hive can spread infections to neighbouring colonies. Swarming, when part of a colony leaves the hive to establish a new one, is a natural process, but a swarm of several thousand bees landing on a busy shopping street can cause alarm. For this reason, beekeeping associations in many cities now require members to complete a training course before they are allowed to install a hive, and some recommend that beginners spend a season helping an experienced keeper first.

Many specialists argue that the most useful thing city dwellers can do for bees is not to keep hives at all, but to plant flowers. Councils in several cities have stopped mowing some grass verges so that wild flowers can grow, and the results have been encouraging: in one trial in Bristol, the number of bees recorded on unmown verges was nearly three times higher than on regularly cut ones. Such measures benefit all pollinators, not just honeybees, and they cost less than the conventional maintenance they replace.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.heading: Sleep and Memory
paragraphs: A

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded by scientists as a passive state, a period in which the brain simply switched off to rest. That view has changed dramatically. Recordings of brain activity show that during certain stages of sleep the brain is extremely busy, and a growing body of research suggests that much of this activity is devoted to processing the experiences of the previous day.
B

Sleep is not a single, uniform state. Over the course of a night, the sleeper passes through a cycle of stages roughly every ninety minutes. In deep, or slow-wave, sleep, brain waves become large and slow, and the body is very difficult to wake. During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, by contrast, the brain is almost as active as when awake, the eyes move quickly beneath closed lids, and most vivid dreaming takes place. Deep sleep dominates the early part of the night, while REM periods become longer towards morning.
C

Evidence that sleep strengthens memory comes from experiments in which volunteers learn a task and are then tested after a period of either sleep or wakefulness. In a typical study, participants who learned a list of word pairs in the evening and slept before being tested remembered around 20 per cent more than those who learned the same list in the morning and were tested after a day awake. Importantly, the advantage remained even when the researchers controlled for the time of day at which testing took place.
D

Researchers believe that different stages of sleep support different kinds of memory. Deep sleep appears to be particularly important for facts and events, the kind of knowledge that can be put into words. During this stage, the hippocampus, a small structure that acts as a temporary store for new information, seems to replay the day's experiences and gradually transfer them to the cortex for long-term storage. REM sleep, on the other hand, has been linked to skills such as playing a musical instrument, and to the ability to find hidden connections between pieces of information.
E

This last finding has intriguing implications for creativity. In one well-known experiment, volunteers were given a mathematical problem that could be solved slowly by following a set of rules, or almost instantly if a hidden shortcut was noticed. After a night's sleep, nearly 60 per cent of participants discovered the shortcut, compared with only about 23 per cent of those who had spent the same period awake. The researchers concluded that sleep does not merely preserve memories but can also reorganise them.
F

These findings matter because many people, students in particular, routinely sacrifice sleep. Surveys suggest that a large proportion of university students sleep less than seven hours a night during examination periods, often in order to revise. The research suggests that this may be counterproductive: staying up late to study may mean that less of what is learned is retained. Some universities have begun to include information about sleep in their study-skills programmes, encouraging students to treat a good night's sleep as part of their preparation rather than as time lost.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.heading: Saving the World's Languages
paragraphs: A

Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around 40 per cent are endangered, and that one language falls silent, on average, every few months. A language is generally considered endangered when children are no longer learning it at home. Once that happens, the number of speakers can only decline as the older generation passes away.
B

The causes of language loss are rarely sudden. In most cases, speakers of a minority language gradually shift to a more widely used language because it offers better access to education, employment and public life. Parents who struggled because they spoke only the local language may decide, with the best of intentions, to raise their children in the national language instead. Within two or three generations, the minority language may survive only among the elderly.
C

Why should this matter to anyone other than the speakers themselves? I would argue that each language represents a unique way of organising human experience. Some languages, for instance, have no words for 'left' and 'right' and describe all positions in terms of compass directions, so that speakers might say that a cup is to the north of a plate. Studies have found that speakers of such languages are remarkably good at keeping track of direction, even in unfamiliar buildings. When a language disappears, insights of this kind may be lost before anyone has had the chance to study them.
D

Languages also carry practical knowledge. Many indigenous languages contain detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, built up over centuries of close observation. Biologists working in the Pacific have, on several occasions, identified new species only after local speakers pointed out distinctions that scientists had overlooked. It would be naive, however, to imagine that this knowledge can always be saved simply by writing down word lists; much of it is embedded in stories, songs and everyday practices that a dictionary cannot capture.
E

Efforts to reverse language decline have had mixed results. The most frequently cited success is Hebrew, which was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries after being used for many centuries mainly in religious and written contexts. In New Zealand, so-called language nests, preschools in which young children are looked after entirely in Māori, helped to create a new generation of speakers from the 1980s onwards. Welsh, too, has benefited from its use in schools and on television and radio, and the number of young people who can speak it has risen.
F

Yet for every success there are many cases in which revival programmes have struggled. Classes for adults often attract enthusiastic learners who nonetheless never reach fluency, and a language that is taught at school but not used at home or in the community may remain a school subject rather than a living language. Funding is another problem: programmes frequently depend on short-term grants, and when these come to an end, progress can be lost.
G

Technology offers new possibilities. Smartphone apps, online dictionaries and social media allow scattered speakers to communicate and allow learners to hear the language spoken. Recordings made today will be available to future generations, even if the language ceases to be spoken. In my view, though, technology cannot replace the one factor that matters most: a community that chooses to use its language in daily life. Without that commitment, even the most sophisticated tools will produce archives rather than speakers.
